A legal move chooses a wall of length n, removes k=1 or 2 consecutive bricks, and leaves wall lengths l and n-k-l, for every integer 0<=l<=n-k; zero lengths are dropped. Existing other walls are unchanged. Sorting loses no legal information because wall locations and orientations do not affect later choices. Every move strictly decreases the total number of bricks. The empty position is losing for the player to move because the preceding player has removed the last brick. For each increasing brick total, declare a state winning if it has a legal successor already proved losing, and losing if every legal successor is proved winning. Induction on the total proves this rule gives a guaranteed strategy, not a random-play probability. Example winning moves from the other choices are A->(1,1,1,4), C->(1,2,2,4), D->(1,1,3,3), and E->(1,2,6). Beth can therefore guarantee a win exactly for B. Both actual images illustrate the same one-wall removal and possible splitting rule. No Sprague-Grundy values, xor-composition theorem or extrapolated periodic pattern is used.
